[Textbook misprint: the stem says "a force of magnitude \(-0.2\) N". A magnitude is never negative; the minus sign is carrying the attractive sense of the force between the unlike charges \(+q\) and \(-2q\). It is read here as an attractive force of magnitude \(0.2\) N, which is what the printed key also assumes.]

[Textbook misprint, corrected above: the length \(BP\) is given in centimetres and was never converted to metres, so the printed working is low by \(10^{4}\) — and the printed final value does not even match that working, the chain reaching \(1.44 \times 10^{3}\) while the answer line prints \(1.44 \times 10^{15}\). Neither is correct. With \(BP = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\) cm \(= 3.54 \times 10^{-2}\) m, \(E = 1.44 \times 10^{7}\) N/C along \(\overrightarrow{BP}\). [Textbook misprint, corrected above: both printed values of the electron-proton force carried the wrong SIGN on the exponent — \(-8.16 \times 10^{8}\) N and \(-8.6 \times 10^{8}\) N — where a force of \(10^{8}\) N between two elementary charges is absurd and the two routes must agree. \(F = qE = 8.16 \times 10^{-8}\) N and Coulomb's law gives \(8.20 \times 10^{-8}\) N, the printed \(8.6\) being a mantissa slip on top of the exponent. The quantity the stem actually asks for, \(E = 5.1 \times 10^{11}\) N/C, is correct and is untouched.]

[Textbook misprint — this question has NO correct option as printed, and is therefore withheld rather than keyed. The forces given are \(80 \times 10^{-3}\) N and \(2.0 \times 10^{-3}\) N, a ratio of \(40\); since \(F \propto 1/r^{2}\) the separation grows by \(\sqrt{40} = 6.32\), which is none of the four alternatives. Two different single-digit repairs each rescue the question and each gives a DIFFERENT answer — reading the first force as \(8.0 \times 10^{-3}\) N gives a ratio of \(4\) and "double the previous distance", while reading the second as \(5.0 \times 10^{-3}\) N gives a ratio of \(16\) and "four times the previous distance". Nothing on the printed page decides between them, so no answer is asserted here. (The charge value of \(+5\ \mu\)C is not needed under any reading; the question is a pure ratio.)]
